- Reassessment does not itself establish that reversing an action is safe; that depends on the current encounter and vessel response.
Source quotations:
- Page 13: Amenity’s master made a quick decision based on scanty information, and did not re-evaluate this decision as more information became apparent.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Being fully laden is treated as proof of confinement to the buoyed channel
- Manoeuvring options are rejected without considering tide and actual depth
Investigator finding: The master incorrectly believed that the laden tanker had to remain within the buoyed channel, although sufficient water existed outside it.
Transferable lesson: Assess navigable manoeuvring space from actual depth, tide, draught and required clearance rather than assuming buoyed limits are absolute physical constraints.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This does not justify leaving a channel where depth, required clearance, local restrictions or other hazards preclude it.
Source quotations:
- Page 10: he considered his vessel to be a fully laden tanker and, in his opinion, this meant that he had no option other than to stay within the buoyed channel
- Page 10: Therefore he had ample water to leave the buoyed channel.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: ineffective_action
Warning signs:
- Astern propulsion is proposed despite a known adverse bow swing
- Opposing helm is assumed to cancel propulsion-induced yaw
Investigator finding: The master's attempt to counter the expected astern-induced port swing with starboard helm did not prevent that swing.
Transferable lesson: Evaluate the combined propulsion and steering response of the vessel when judging a proposed avoidance action; do not assume opposing helm will cancel astern-induced yaw.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The direction and magnitude of this response are vessel-specific and must not be transferred to different propulsion or steering arrangements.
Source quotations:
- Page 1: in an attempt to counter the port swing that this would induce, he put the steering hard to starboard. However, Amenity turned to port
- Page 10: In this perceived emergency situation, Amenity’s master’s decision to go astern is questionable.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Vessel remains on the wrong side of a channel as traffic approaches
- Mid-channel navigation is not adjusted to leave passing space
Investigator finding: Amenity approached on the wrong side of the channel despite instructions to keep to starboard unless otherwise agreed.
Transferable lesson: Check channel position against local navigation instructions and the space needed for approaching traffic, rather than continuing a clear-water positioning practice into an encounter.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific side-of-channel instruction applies only where equivalent requirements exist and no contrary agreement applies.
Source quotations:
- Page 9: Leading up to the collision, Amenity was positioned towards the wrong side of the channel.
- Page 9: Pilots and PEC holders are instructed to keep to the starboard side of the channel unless agreement has been made to the contrary

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Turning through the wakes of other boats
- Bow dropping, speed reducing and turn tightening
Investigator finding: During A89's attempted tighter exit from the corner, wakes from two boats affected it; its bow dropped, speed fell and turn tightened, consistent with a moderate hook.
Transferable lesson: For comparable fast-boat manoeuvres, include wake-induced handling changes in the assessment of a proposed turn and the predictability of nearby boats.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This mechanism is not established for dissimilar vessel types or manoeuvres without comparable wake exposure.
- The report does not quantify wake limits or prescribe a turn geometry.
Source quotations:
- Page 7: In doing so, the boat was affected by the wakes of boats B27 and A28.
- Page 7: The bow of A89 dropped, the boat slowed down and turned more tightly than was needed to follow the course, consistent with it having suffered a moderate hook.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Many boats sharing a short, demanding course
- Limited space to manoeuvre
- A high proportion of inexperienced crews
Investigator finding: Course design combined with the number of boats reduced manoeuvring space and safety margins, placing greater demands on inexperienced racers, although a direct contribution of the course to the collision could not be shown.
Transferable lesson: Assess manoeuvring proposals against the combined demands of traffic density, available space and crew experience, not simply whether an individual manoeuvre is physically possible.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The report does not prove that course design directly caused this collision.
- The finding does not establish numerical traffic-density or separation limits for other waters.
Source quotations:
- Page 6: The combination of course design and the number of boats racing meant that each boat had less space to manoeuvre.
- Page 9: While it is not possible to show that the Dover course contributed directly to the collision, it is considered that the combination of course design and the number of boats racing put greater demands on the inexperienced racers taking part, and reduced safety margins.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Departure in severely restricted visibility with an approaching vessel already reported.
- Schedule delay influencing the decision to sail.
Investigator finding: The decision to sail in restricted visibility, despite the opportunity to wait for approaching traffic to clear, contributed to the collision; schedule pressure was also identified as a cause.
Transferable lesson: When considering departure into restricted visibility and known approaching traffic, assess the option of waiting clear of the encounter without allowing schedule pressure to determine the decision.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific waiting-alongside analogy does not transfer when already underway or when remaining alongside is not a safe available option.
Source quotations:
- Page 21: The skipper was unwise to sail in such circumstances.
- Page 21: Had he waited until Nordsee was past and clear, the accident would have been avoided.
- Page 25: Poole Scene being 30 minutes behind schedule.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: inadequate_cpa_assessment, poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- An apparently clear passing arrangement is accepted without radar plotting.
- A small estimated CPA is treated as sufficient without continuous assessment.
Investigator finding: Both vessels accepted an approximately 0.1-mile CPA without a radar plot; continuous monitoring including plotting could have given earlier warning.
Transferable lesson: Use systematic radar plotting and continuous monitoring to test an assumed safe pass rather than relying on an initial impression of clearance.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The finding does not establish a universal minimum CPA.
- The radar-specific lesson does not transfer where radar information is unavailable.
Source quotations:
- Page 22: All concerned were content with a CPA of approximately 0.1 mile and the speed their vessels were making.
- Page 22: No attempt was made to carry out a radar plot, or to reduce speed.
- Page 24: A radar plot, conducted on both vessels, could have provided advanced warning of the collision.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: inadequate_cpa_assessment, delayed_action
Warning signs:
- Limited passing clearance in restricted visibility.
- Little time remains to assess the encounter or respond.
Investigator finding: A greater CPA and reduced speed would have provided more assessment and avoiding-action time.
Transferable lesson: Assess proposed clearance and speed together for whether they preserve sufficient time to understand and respond to a developing encounter.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This finding supplies neither a numerical safe CPA nor a prescribed speed for another encounter.
- Its direct context is restricted visibility, not a universal assessment of all passing arrangements.
Source quotations:
- Page 23: Had a greater CPA and a reduction in speed been adopted in accordance with Rules 6a (i), (ii), b (i) and 8 (e), more time to fully assess the situation and to take avoiding action would have been available.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, delayed_action
Warning signs:
- A vessel's radar echo merges with a buoy echo.
- The contact can no longer be distinguished separately.
Investigator finding: When Nordsee's echo merged with Whiteforeland Buoy, Poole Scene's skipper should have treated the closest edge as Nordsee and taken avoiding action.
Transferable lesson: When a tracked vessel merges with a fixed-target echo, assess the hazard conservatively using the closest edge rather than treating the vessel's position as safely resolved.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This specific interpretation applies to merged echoes involving a known vessel and fixed target, not every unexplained radar return.
Source quotations:
- Page 22: when the echo of Nordsee merged with that of Whiteforeland Buoy he should have interpreted that the closest edge of the echo was Nordsee and taken avoiding action.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, ineffective_action
Warning signs:
- Contact tracking is lost at close range.
- Attempts to take way off begin only after vessels are already very close.
Investigator finding: Attempts to take way off came too late at close proximity; the report also found that astern propulsion on Nordsee might have prevented the collision.
Transferable lesson: Assess whether the timing and effectiveness of the proposed propulsion response are sufficient to remove way before close proximity makes the response ineffective.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The report does not establish that astern propulsion is the appropriate response in every encounter.
- Effectiveness depends on the vessel's propulsion response and the remaining time and separation.
Source quotations:
- Page 22: Attempts were made to take the way off each vessel but, because of their close proximity, it was too late to avoid a collision.
- Page 24: The use of astern propulsion on Nordsee might have prevented the collision.

report_title: Alam Pintar / Etoile des Ondes Report No 11/2010
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: ineffective_action, poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- A fishing vessel changes course or speed.
- An initially improving encounter deteriorates again.
Investigator finding: Fishing operations can require abrupt course and speed changes that cancel insubstantial avoiding action, especially when little time remains.
Transferable lesson: Do not extrapolate a fishing contact's current motion as necessarily steady; closely monitor whether avoiding action remains effective as its operation changes.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The fishing-specific explanation does not establish that an arbitrary non-fishing contact will manoeuvre similarly.
- It does not predict the next course or speed of a fishing vessel.
Source quotations:
- Page 18: Watchkeepers on merchant vessels should be aware that a vessel engaged in fishing may make sudden changes of course and speed, depending on the stage of the fishing operation.
- Page 18: These changes could cancel out insubstantial actions to avoid collision, especially if taken too late, when there is little chance to take additional action.

report_title: Alam Pintar / Etoile des Ondes Report No 11/2010
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, inadequate_cpa_assessment
Warning signs:
- A detected contact has not been monitored during fishing or repositioning.
- A brief visual check is being used to judge an approaching vessel's proximity.
Investigator finding: The skipper did not monitor Alam Pintar and failed to appreciate its avoiding actions or proximity; a quick visual check without radar was insufficient.
Transferable lesson: Maintain assessment of detected traffic throughout operational tasks and repositioning; do not substitute a brief visual check for an updated appraisal of a developing encounter.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This finding does not mean that every visual observation requires radar confirmation or that radar alone is sufficient.
Source quotations:
- Page 16: A quick visual check, without referring to the radar, was insufficient to fully appreciate how close Alam Pintar now was.
- Page 23: Although Alam Pintar had been seen, her actions were not monitored

report_title: Alam Pintar / Etoile des Ondes Report No 11/2010
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: inadequate_cpa_assessment, other
Warning signs:
- A proposal to begin shooting relies on another vessel altering.
- The approaching vessel's proximity has not been comprehensively assessed.
Investigator finding: Resuming shooting on the assumption that Alam Pintar would alter was ill considered.
Transferable lesson: Before starting a fishing operation that changes the encounter, establish that it is safe rather than relying on an expected avoiding action by the approaching vessel; defer commencement while collision risk remains unresolved.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This lesson concerns deciding whether to commence an operation, not prescribing how to manoeuvre once gear already constrains the vessel.
Source quotations:
- Page 17: The decision to resume shooting was based on the assumption that Alam Pintar would alter to starboard, and was ill considered.
- Page 17: it might have been prudent to delay shooting until it had been established that there was no risk of collision.

report_title: Alam Pintar / Etoile des Ondes Report No 11/2010
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact, unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: poor_team_coordination, delayed_action
Warning signs:
- The OOW is unsure of a contact's intentions.
- Nearby traffic appears to constrain avoiding action.
- The OOW has limited experience.
Investigator finding: The inexperienced OOW did not consider calling the master despite uncertainty; the analysis identified an early opportunity to seek assistance when adjacent traffic might have constrained action.
Transferable lesson: Seek the master's assistance early when uncertainty or surrounding traffic exceeds the OOW's ability to resolve the encounter confidently.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- Calling the master is not evidence that immediate collision-avoidance responsibilities can be deferred.
Source quotations:
- Page 23: The OOW on Alam Pintar lacked experience and was unsure about the actions of Etoile des Ondes, however he did not consider calling the master for assistance.
- Page 17: It is possible the OOW did not take more substantial action as he was concerned not to stray across the path of other vessels navigating alongside his vessel.
- Page 17: it would have been entirely reasonable, even at this early stage, for him to have called the master.

report_title: Alam Pintar / Etoile des Ondes Report No 11/2010
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Bright working lights obscure navigation lights.
- Working-light glare affects the watchkeeper's night vision.
Investigator finding: Powerful deck lighting impeded identification of the fishing vessel's navigation lights and probably impaired its skipper's night vision.
Transferable lesson: Treat working-light glare as a limitation on visual identification and detection, and protect watchkeepers' night vision when evaluating traffic.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This is a darkness and glare limitation, not evidence of meteorological restricted visibility.
- It does not establish that a particular light configuration identifies a vessel's status.
Source quotations:
- Page 17: The OOW also found it difficult to identify the fishing vessel’s navigation lights against the high powered halogen deck lights.
- Page 17: Etoile des Ondes’ powerful deck lights probably impaired the skipper’s night vision.
- Page 17: Glare from the working lights could have reduced the distance from which other vessels could be identified.

report_title: Alam Pintar / Etoile des Ondes Report No 11/2010
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, other
Warning signs:
- Structural modifications restrict rearward visibility.
- An approaching vessel's actions may fall within an obstructed sector.
Investigator finding: The effect of modifications on rearward visibility was not fully assessed and probably hindered observation of Alam Pintar's actions.
Transferable lesson: Include known visibility obstructions in the lookout assessment rather than treating an unobserved manoeuvre as evidence that no manoeuvre occurred.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific rearward blind-sector concern does not transfer to a vessel without comparable obstructions.
Source quotations:
- Page 23: The effect of the modifications on rearward visibility was not fully assessed and probably made it difficult for the skipper to see the actions taken by Alam Pintar.

report_title: Alam Pintar / Etoile des Ondes Report No 11/2010
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: overtaking
Vessel roles: overtaking_vessel, stand_on
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: role_confusion, other
Warning signs:
- A fishing vessel is repositioning without outlying gear.
- Displayed fishing lights may not reflect its current operational status.
Investigator finding: Even if Etoile des Ondes was not engaged in fishing during repositioning, Alam Pintar still had to keep clear as the overtaking vessel; appropriate lights and steady motion would have aided assessment.
Transferable lesson: Assess overtaking obligations separately from fishing status, and ensure that displayed status and vessel conduct reflect the actual operational phase.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The overtaking conclusion applies only where overtaking is established.
- The discussion of extinguishing fishing lights and maintaining motion concerned the interval without outlying gear, not active constrained fishing.
Source quotations:
- Page 16: However, as she was then being overtaken, she should still have been afforded the protection of COLREGS - Rule 13 (Annex 7), and Alam Pintar was still required to keep clear of her.
- Page 16: it would have been the fishing vessel’s responsibility to switch off her fishing lights, and as many of her deck lights as practicable, and maintain her course and speed
- Page 16: This would have helped Alam Pintar’s OOW to make a better assessment of her actions.

report_title: Homeland and Scottish Viking Report No 4/2011
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Wheelhouse intermittently unattended
- Lookout position has obstructed all-round visibility
Investigator finding: Intermittent wheelhouse checks and a lookout from the sheltered aft deck did not provide adequate detection of collision risk.
Transferable lesson: Maintain a continuous, effective lookout from a position with adequate visibility and access to available navigational aids; intermittent checks are not a substitute.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific obstructed-position analogy does not apply where a continuous, effective lookout is maintained elsewhere.
Source quotations:
- Page 11: the wheelhouse was not being manned continuously
- Page 11: The skipper and Daniel had been standing on the aft deck within a shelter that significantly restricted their all-round view.
- Page 16: these checks were insufficiently thorough to identify a risk of collision with Scottish Viking.

report_title: Homeland and Scottish Viking Report No 4/2011
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, inadequate_cpa_assessment
Warning signs:
- Radar operating only on a short range scale
- Rapidly approaching traffic may remain outside the displayed range
Investigator finding: Homeland's short radar range provided very little warning of the approaching ferry; long-range scanning should have been used.
Transferable lesson: Include long-range radar scanning in risk assessment so that range selection does not conceal approaching traffic until little response time remains.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The short-range-display mechanism does not apply when adequate longer-range surveillance is already maintained.
- The reported three-minute warning interval is specific to this encounter's relative motion.
Source quotations:
- Page 12: This should have included the use of long-range radar scanning to provide an early warning of the risk of collision
- Page 12: Scottish Viking’s radar echo would not have appeared on Homeland’s radar display until about 3 minutes before impact.

report_title: Homeland and Scottish Viking Report No 4/2011
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact, crossing
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, inadequate_cpa_assessment
Warning signs:
- Several contacts visually observed without systematic bearing measurements or radar tracking
- Binocular observation treated as sufficient risk assessment
Investigator finding: The second officer relied on binocular observation rather than measured bearing trends or radar plotting to assess the fishing vessels.
Transferable lesson: Establish collision risk through systematic bearing observations or radar tracking rather than relying solely on an impression of visual movement, especially among multiple contacts.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This criticism does not transfer to visual observation supported by systematic bearing measurements and adequate risk assessment.
Source quotations:
- Page 13: Instead, he chose to visually monitor the fishing vessels using a pair of binoculars.
- Page 12: Taken a series of visual compass bearings using the starboard azimuth ring
- Page 12: Monitored or plotted the radar’s targets using the cursor or ARPA facility.

report_title: Homeland and Scottish Viking Report No 4/2011
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: crossing
Vessel roles: give_way
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, poor_team_coordination
Warning signs:
- Autopilot remains engaged as collision risk becomes apparent
- OOW must both change steering arrangements and monitor a developing encounter
Investigator finding: Earlier placement of the vessel in hand steering with the AB on the wheel would have enabled immediate execution while preserving the officer's ability to monitor.
Transferable lesson: Prepare steering control and bridge task allocation in time to execute collision-avoidance decisions without interrupting situational monitoring.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific hand-steering lesson depends on the vessel's control arrangements, available personnel and applicable procedures.
Source quotations:
- Page 14: Had the second officer placed the vessel in hand steering and put the AB on the wheel as soon as he had assessed there was a risk of collision, any decision to alter course could have been enacted immediately and without compromising his ability to monitor the situation.

report_title: Homeland and Scottish Viking Report No 4/2011
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: crossing
Vessel roles: stand_on
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, delayed_action
Warning signs:
- Give-way vessel is not resolving the danger
- Risk recognised only at the last moment
Investigator finding: Homeland's stand-on status did not remove the obligation to act when the give-way vessel alone could no longer avoid collision; its skipper's response was too late.
Transferable lesson: Continue assessing risk while standing on and recognise the point at which action is needed to aid avoidance before intervention becomes ineffective.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The stand-on obligation described applies only where that role is established.
- The report does not establish deliberate rigid adherence to stand-on status as Homeland's cause.
Source quotations:
- Page 14: when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel alone, Rule 17(b) requires the stand-on vessel to “ take such action as will best aid to avoid collision”.
- Page 14: However, these actions were too late to be effective.

report_title: Homeland and Scottish Viking Report No 4/2011
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: crossing
Vessel roles: give_way
Encounter phases: action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Whistle used to attract attention with a signal conveying a different manoeuvre
Investigator finding: The officer used one short blast as an attention-getting signal instead of the prescribed warning; its understood meaning could have discouraged useful action by another vessel.
Transferable lesson: Use the appropriate sound signal for the intended warning or manoeuvre; do not substitute a manoeuvring signal as a generic attention call.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The cited signalling requirements concern vessels in sight of one another, not restricted-visibility signalling.
Source quotations:
- Page 15: the second officer should have sounded at least five short and rapid blasts on the whistle in accordance with Rule 34(d).
- Page 15: his one short blast, meaning ‘I am altering my course to starboard’ could have deterred a stand-on vessel from reducing speed or altering course to port for fear of creating a head-on collision.

report_title: Homeland and Scottish Viking Report No 4/2011
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown, multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, inadequate_cpa_assessment
Warning signs:
- Attention confined to AIS-labelled contacts
- Unlabelled radar echoes not assessed
- Total reliance on either AIS or ARPA
Investigator finding: AIS and ARPA are complementary and fallible; AIS-focused interrogation can cause other radar contacts to be ignored.
Transferable lesson: Cross-check complementary tracking information and assess relevant radar contacts whether or not they carry AIS symbols.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- Absence of AIS alone does not establish collision risk.
- This is not a reason to discard useful AIS information.
Source quotations:
- Page 15: AIS does not replace, but supports radar tracking.
- Page 15: OOWs should not place total reliance on either one because both are prone to errors.
- Page 15: only targets with AIS symbols warrant interrogation, with all other targets on the radar display being ignored without determining if they actually pose a danger.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- High-speed night operation without navigation lights.
- Local familiarity offered as reassurance despite missing collision-prevention safeguards.
Investigator finding: The investigator rejected local knowledge as a substitute for COLREG compliance and identified the risks of allowing high-speed craft to operate at night without navigation lights.
Transferable lesson: Do not accept local knowledge as justification for operating without required navigation lights or other applicable collision-prevention safeguards.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The missing-light aspect does not transfer where appropriate navigation lights are displayed; this finding does not establish encounter roles or a particular avoidance manoeuvre.
Source quotations:
- Page 11: Good local knowledge of a particular area does not obviate the fundamental requirement to comply with the CO/REGS.
- Page 11: the CBYC chief instructor was content to allow high speed power-driven craft to operate at night, without navigation lights

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_team_coordination
Warning signs:
- Several high-speed craft crossing the same area in darkness without coordination.
Investigator finding: The investigator identified a failure to recognise the risks of four high-speed RIBs crossing the bay in darkness in an uncoordinated manner.
Transferable lesson: For associated craft operating together at night, include coordination of their movements in the collision-risk controls rather than treating each passage in isolation.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The group-coordination analogy does not transfer to a lone craft or imply that unrelated traffic can be controlled as a coordinated group.
Source quotations:
- Page 11: a failure to recognise the risks associated with four high speed RIBs crossing the bay in darkness in an uncoordinated manner.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: crossing
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- A planned TSS crossing runs contrary to traffic flow.
- Commercial pressure favours a non-compliant shortcut.
Investigator finding: Non-compliant crossing undermined the predictability provided by the TSS; commercial interests had taken precedence over compliance.
Transferable lesson: Keep TSS compliance a planning constraint rather than trading predictable traffic behaviour for commercial advantage.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The TSS-specific lesson does not apply outside a traffic separation scheme.
Source quotations:
- Page 26: A fundamental purpose of the Collision Regulations and TSS is to improve safety at sea by requiring vessels to behave in a predictable manner.
- Page 33: Compliance with Rule 10 of the Collision Regulations was a lesser consideration than commercial interests

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: inadequate_cpa_assessment
Warning signs:
- A contact requires CPA assessment and detection of subsequent alterations.
Investigator finding: The OOW's systematic use of semi-automatic radar followed manual-plotting principles and provided a quick, accurate CPA assessment.
Transferable lesson: Judge radar assessment by systematic relative-motion observation and its ability to establish CPA and reveal alterations, not solely by automation level.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This finding does not validate unsystematic observation or unreliable radar data.
Source quotations:
- Page 27: the OOW’s use of the semi-automatic radar to monitor Saint Jacques II, and determine if a risk of collision existed, followed the same principles as manual plotting.
- Page 27: This resulted in a quick and accurate assessment of her CPA, and would have provided an early detection of course alterations.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact, crossing
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: inadequate_cpa_assessment, poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Ships lie on similar bearings.
- Visual aspect conflicts with the tracked contact.
- A larger or brighter ship appears to be the nearer radar target.
Investigator finding: The deckhand may have associated another vessel's lights with the nearest radar contact, and assessed both vessels' CPAs inaccurately.
Transferable lesson: Resolve visual-to-radar identity ambiguities separately for each nearby contact before relying on aspect changes or an apparent safe passage.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The contact-confusion analogy does not apply where target identity is positively established and maintained.
Source quotations:
- Page 28: either the deckhand’s assessment of the lights he saw was incorrect, or the lights observed were those of another ship, possibly Romandie.
- Page 28: With Gudermes and Romandie on similar bearings and within a mile of each other
- Page 33: The deckhand’s assessment of the CPA of Gudermes and Romandie was inaccurate.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: crossing, multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, inadequate_cpa_assessment
Warning signs:
- An initial safe-passing assessment is no longer being checked.
- Range decreases on a steady bearing.
Investigator finding: Continuous lookout should have exposed the erroneous passing assessments in time for avoiding action.
Transferable lesson: Continue checking bearing, range and CPA after an initial safe-passing assessment; do not treat that assessment as closing the contact.
Do not transfer this analogy when:

Encounter types: multi_contact, unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, distraction
Warning signs:

- Dense traffic would generate frequent long-range alarms.
Investigator finding: Long-range guard zones could be distracting in dense traffic, whereas close-range zones could warn of dangerously close vessels without normally producing numerous alarms.
Transferable lesson: Consider close-range guard zones as a supplementary proximity warning, while assessing alarm burden before using wider zones in dense traffic.
Do not transfer this analogy when:

Vessel roles: stand_on, give_way
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: role_confusion

- TSS non-compliance creates uncertainty about obligations.
Investigator finding: The TSS contravention did not remove the crossing situation or its stand-on and give-way responsibilities.

- Unexpected against-flow movement delays assessment.

Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This does not justify disregarding stand-on obligations where the other vessel is taking appropriate action.
- It does not prescribe a particular manoeuvre.

text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, ineffective_action, poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- High closing speed at close range
- Collision risk recognised only after a turn
- Helmsman surprised by a contact's proximity
- Proposed avoidance depends on completing a manoeuvre within little remaining time
Investigator finding: Closing speed left N207 insufficient time to complete its avoidance turn. Investigators also identified surprise as a possible source of delayed avoidance and disrupted problem solving on Rescue 1.
Transferable lesson: Assess whether an avoidance proposal can take effect within the remaining closing time, allowing for recognition and execution delay; do not assume a late response will be effective merely because action has begun.

- The report provides no numerical reaction-time or manoeuvring threshold for other vessels.

Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Rain showers
- Wipers smearing windows
- Reluctance to use outside observing positions
Investigator finding: Weather hampered the visual lookout; wiper movement and smearing could hinder observation, and showers discouraged going outside.

Encounter types: unknown

Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, other
Warning signs:
- Frequent rain or sea clutter adjustments
- Small close-range contact absent from radar
Investigator finding: Clutter suppression might have been increased enough to prevent detection of a small vessel at close range.

- The specific suppression concern does not transfer where suitable settings and target detection have been established.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown

Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, other
Warning signs:

- Poor short-range reception
- Poor pictures in rain and sea interference
Investigator finding: The radars' condition might have prevented a satisfactory radar watch, and the other vessel might not have been detected on either set.

Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Long range selected to work around equipment problems
- Attention focused away from the radar centre
- Uneven attention between radar sets
Investigator finding: A small close-range target might have been less apparent on the longer radar range, and concentrating on one set might have missed a target on the other.
Transferable lesson: Ensure radar range selection and allocation of attention preserve close-range contact detection as well as longer-range awareness.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific comparison between the two radar sets does not transfer where their ranges, performance, and use differ.

Encounter types: overtaking, multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Busiest or narrowest part of transit just completed
- Surrounding traffic moving in the same direction
Investigator finding: Vigilance might have fallen after the busiest, narrowest part of the Strait and because surrounding traffic was travelling in the same direction.
Transferable lesson: Do not relax contact monitoring merely because traffic is co-directional or the most demanding part of a transit appears complete.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This is a possible vigilance mechanism, not evidence that every co-directional encounter is dangerous.

Transferable lesson: Use closing speed and range trends to determine assessment urgency; broadly similar courses do not remove the need for early appraisal.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The reported speeds and time margins are not universal action thresholds.
Source quotations:

Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Slow own-vessel progress

Investigator finding: Slow vessels are frequently approached from astern, making a good visual lookout astern crucial.
Transferable lesson: Include the stern sector in systematic visual monitoring rather than concentrating solely on contacts ahead.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific frequency of overtaking approaches need not transfer to stationary vessels or traffic settings without faster following vessels.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: overtaking
Vessel roles: stand_on
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, rigid_stand_on_interpretation
Warning signs:

- Waiting despite increasing concern
- Fear of conflicting with a possible last-minute manoeuvre
Investigator finding: Hampoel's stand-on status did not remove her risk-assessment and action responsibilities; she failed to act despite being permitted and subsequently required to do so.
Transferable lesson: Reassess stand-on obligations as the encounter develops; expected action by the overtaking vessel is not a substitute for timely assessment of one's own duties.

Vessel roles: stand_on
Encounter phases: action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, ineffective_action
Warning signs:
- Unanswered VHF call
- Whistle warning deferred until collision is imminent
- Approaching vessel apparently unaware of own vessel
Investigator finding: The VHF call was unlikely to produce an immediate response; a light shown astern was more likely to attract attention, and the whistle was sounded too late.
Transferable lesson: Do not let an attempted VHF exchange delay timely warning signals or necessary collision-avoidance action; consider the effectiveness of available attention-getting signals.

- The specific comparison with a light shown astern concerns an approaching vessel astern and does not prescribe that signal for every geometry.

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD

MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD

report_title: MAIBInvReport 7/2020 - ANL Wyong and King Arthur - Serious Marine Casualty
text:

Encounter types: stationary_contact, multi_contact, restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, other
Warning signs:
- Increasing traffic approaching a waiting vessel
- OOW expects other vessels to keep clear despite evident collision risk
Investigator finding: ANL Wyong’s OOW recognised the developing traffic situation but did not act because he expected approaching vessels to keep clear.
Transferable lesson: Being stopped or waiting for port instructions is not a basis for leaving collision avoidance entirely to approaching vessels; reassess the need for action as traffic develops.

- Page 12: ANL Wyong’s OOW was keeping an effective lookout and aware of the developing situation but did not act to avoid collision

report_title: MAIBInvReport 7/2020 - ANL Wyong and King Arthur - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact, multi_contact, restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, other
Warning signs:
- Own vessel stopped while multiple contacts approach
- Available avoiding-action options diminishing
Investigator finding: Remaining stopped as traffic approached deprived ANL Wyong’s OOW of avoiding-action options; being stopped was not a safe speed in those circumstances.
Transferable lesson: Assess a stopped waiting condition against the manoeuvring options it preserves as traffic changes; zero speed is not automatically a safe control state.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- Does not imply that stopping is generally unsafe or that making way is always appropriate.
- Applies where the stopped condition materially limits effective avoiding action.
Source quotations:
- Page 14: remaining stopped when multiple contacts were approaching resulted in a situation where the OOW had no options available to take avoiding action.
- Page 14: being stopped in the water in dense fog and heavy shipping was, in effect, not proceeding at a safe speed

report_title: MAIBInvReport 7/2020 - ANL Wyong and King Arthur - Serious Marine Casualty
text:

Warning signs:
- Speed driven by transfer arrival time
- Dense fog and heavy shipping leave little assessment time

- Page 14: King Arthur was proceeding at about 13kts, which was the speed required to arrive at the boat transfer position on time.

Warning signs:
- Vessel within a VTS sector but outside its operational focus
- No shore warning despite developing collision risk
Investigator finding: The collision area was not routinely monitored by either relevant VTS, and neither vessel received a shore warning.
Transferable lesson: Do not treat VTS coverage or silence from shore as confirmation that the traffic situation is safe; retain independent onboard collision-risk assessment.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- Does not establish that all VTS areas have the monitoring gaps found here.
- Does not negate the value of shore information when provided.
Source quotations:

report_title: MAIBInvReport 6/2020 - Red Falcon and Greylag - Very Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown, restricted_visibility
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, other
Warning signs:
- Change between control stations
- Heading display dependent on a manual switch
- Displayed orientation conflicts with other instruments
Investigator finding: The master did not operate the manual heading-selection switch when changing ends, and erroneous ECS heading information reinforced his mistaken understanding of travel direction.
Transferable lesson: After a control-station or operating-direction change, verify heading-display configuration and reconcile orientation with independent instruments before relying on the chart symbol.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The manual-switch mechanism is specific to systems with comparable heading-selection arrangements; it should not be presumed on other vessels.

- Page 19: The erroneous heading information being displayed supported the master’s belief that he was driving Red Falcon back into the channel.
- Page 17: the master completely ignored the radar and digital compass, which gave the correct orientation

report_title: MAIBInvReport 4/2026 - Apache/Serinah - Very Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: inadequate_cpa_assessment
Warning signs:
- Approaching contact remains on a steady bearing.
- Uncertainty persists about whether collision risk exists.
Investigator finding: A steady bearing visible from Apache's bridge indicated collision risk long before impact; doubt should have been treated as risk.
Transferable lesson: Treat a steady bearing or unresolved doubt as requiring collision-risk assessment rather than reassurance from uncertain intentions.

- The steady-bearing indicator does not establish risk for a contact that is not approaching; assess the actual relative motion.

report_title: MAIBInvReport 4/2026 - Apache/Serinah - Very Serious Marine Casualty

text:

- A warning signal is deferred until collision is imminent.

report_title: MAIB Report 5/2020 - Gülnak and Cape Mathilde - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Higher approach speed where safe water for recovery is limited.
Investigator finding: The higher speed at the start of the turn reduced the time and safe water available to respond to loss of control, although it should not have adversely affected steering.
Transferable lesson: Include the time and safe-water margin for recovering from an unexpected manoeuvring response when assessing an approach speed, rather than considering steering effectiveness alone.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The finding does not establish a generally applicable speed limit.
- It does not support attributing a steering failure to speed alone.
Source quotations:
- Page 6: Although a faster speed would have reduced the time and safe water available to react to the loss of control, it should not have adversely affected the vessel’s steering.

report_title: MAIB Report 5/2020 - Gülnak and Cape Mathilde - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: action_required, emergency
Causal mechanisms: ineffective_action
Warning signs:
- An intended turn continues despite countermeasures.
- Available recovery time is being consumed while waiting for control inputs to take effect.
Investigator finding: The pilot and master recognised the unexpected turn promptly and applied countermeasures consistent with usual practice, but those measures did not restore control in time.
Transferable lesson: Judge corrective action by the measured vessel response and remaining clearance, not solely by whether the action is prompt or normally effective; retain contingency awareness while waiting for its effect.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This does not establish that the same countermeasures will fail in another encounter.
- The report does not identify an alternative manoeuvre that would have prevented this collision.
Source quotations:
- Page 7: The pilot and the master were quick to realise that Gülnak’s intended turn to port towards the Redcar bulk terminal was not progessing as planned.
- Page 7: In most cases, such actions are likely to be successful.
- Page 7: However, in this case, they were not, despite the pilot and the master allowing about 1.5 minutes for the counter-measures to take effect.

report_title: MAIB Report 5/2020 - Gülnak and Cape Mathilde - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- An engine command produces no immediate increase in vessel speed.
- Turning and substantial rudder application are occurring simultaneously with a propulsion increase.
Investigator finding: The lack of an immediate vessel-speed increase probably reflected engine response time, speed loss in the turn and rudder drag; the subsequent reduction in turn rate indicated increased propeller flow improving rudder effectiveness.
Transferable lesson: Distinguish an engine command from its achieved effect, and assess propulsion response using both engine information and motion trends rather than speed alone.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This explanation does not rule out propulsion or indication faults in another case.
- It does not establish a universal engine response time.
Source quotations:
- Page 7: this was probably due to the designed response time of the engine and the speed lost while turning along with the drag of full starboard rudder.
- Page 7: The reduction in the rate of turn after the engine speed was reported to have reached 90rpm also indicates that an increased water flow from the propeller was making the rudder more effective.

report_title: MAIB Report 5/2020 - Gülnak and Cape Mathilde - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: other
Warning signs:
- Unexpected directional response in depth-limited water.
- Dynamic trim or squat may differ from the static loading condition.
Investigator finding: Shallow-water influence could not be excluded despite UKC exceeding 8m; any such effect might have been exacerbated by the vessel trimming by the head while moving ahead.
Transferable lesson: When directional response is unexpected, consider dynamic trim and squat as well as nominal UKC; a seemingly generous absolute UKC does not by itself exclude shallow-water influence.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- Shallow-water effects were a possibility, not an identified cause.
- This analogy does not apply where depth-related interaction is irrelevant, and it does not support assuming bank effects merely because a vessel is in a channel.
Source quotations:
- Page 8: Although the minimum UKC experienced exceeded 8m, the possibility that Gülnak’s heading and directional stability were influenced to some degree by shallow water effects cannot be eliminated.
- Page 7: any shallow water effect might have been exacerbated by Gülnak trimming by the head when moving ahead, which would have increased the squat at the bow.

report_title: MAIB Report 10/2019 - Tiger One - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, other
Warning signs:
- Electronic position information is available but not being consulted.
- Display dimming for night vision makes the navigation aid effectively unused.
- High-speed operation leaves little capacity to consult navigation equipment while looking ahead.
Investigator finding: The chart plotter would have revealed the boat's position and approach towards the buoys, but neither crew member consulted it; using it at high speed would also have competed with looking ahead.
Transferable lesson: Ensure available position information can actually be used to cross-check hazard clearance without compromising the forward lookout; equipment availability alone is not an effective navigation safeguard.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific display-use problem does not transfer where position information is already effectively monitored.
- The report does not establish radar, AIS or target-tracking performance limitations.
Source quotations:
- Page 8: Although the chart plotter would have shown that Tiger One was on the starboard side of the channel, and was heading towards the UST and LST mooring buoys, the skipper and deckhand did not look at it because it was dimmed to protect their night vision.
- Page 8: Its use at high speed would also have been challenging due to the importance of the skipper keeping his focus ahead.

report_title: MAIB Report 10/2019 - Tiger One - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, other
Warning signs:
- Continuing a high-speed transit before known hazards have been positively sighted.
- Passenger comfort or schedule considerations favour maintaining progress despite uncertain hazard clearance.
Investigator finding: The skipper consciously maintained speed to disembark cold passengers sooner; investigators considered slowing for the transit until the buoys were sighted appropriate. Detection ultimately occurred too late for avoiding action.
Transferable lesson: Make the adequacy of detection and available avoidance time a condition for continuing a transit, rather than allowing passenger-comfort pressure to override unresolved hazard clearance.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This finding does not prescribe a particular speed or manoeuvre for another encounter.
- The analogy is limited where hazards are already reliably located and adequate avoidance time is established.
Source quotations:
- Page 8: In the cold conditions, the skipper opted to maintain speed so he could disembark the passengers as soon as possible.
- Page 8: In the circumstances, slowing the RIB for the transit of Greenwich Reach, until the Ship Tier buoys were sighted, would have been appropriate.
- Page 9: Tiger One collided with the outer LST buoy because its skipper did not see the buoy until it was so close it became too late to take avoiding action.

report_title: MAIB Report 4/2019 - Red Falcon and Phoenix - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact, overtaking
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- A previously discounted slow-moving contact increases speed or enters the intended channel.
- An assessment relies on the contact remaining outside the channel or on own vessel holding a heading only briefly.
Investigator finding: The ferry's initial assessment discounted the recreational craft, and its master did not notice Phoenix's subsequent speed and entry into the channel.
Transferable lesson: Reassess previously discounted contacts as their motion and relationship to the intended track change; do not carry forward an assessment based on their earlier speed or location.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific stale-assessment mechanism does not apply where the contact's current motion and channel entry have already been detected and reassessed.
Source quotations:
- Page 4: The master’s assessment that none of these craft were of concern was probably based on their slow speed, that they were outside the main channel, and that the ferry would be steadying on its new heading for only a short period.
- Page 4: He did not notice that Phoenix, which had seemingly briefly reduced speed between 1627 and 1632, was making good almost 8kts and was also entering the Thorn Channel.

report_title: MAIB Report 4/2019 - Red Falcon and Phoenix - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring, distraction
Warning signs:
- Bridge attention is concentrated on a contact obstructing the next intended alteration.
- Maintaining the present heading competes with monitoring other sectors.
Investigator finding: The bridge team's focus on a yacht to port contributed to its failure to detect Phoenix on the starboard bow; the chief officer also had heading-control demands.
Transferable lesson: When one contact constrains the intended manoeuvre, preserve lookout coverage of other sectors rather than allowing that contact and vessel-control tasks to absorb the team's attention.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- This attention-allocation analogy does not apply where no competing contact or control task is narrowing lookout coverage.
Source quotations:
- Page 7: Red Falcon’s master and chief officer were focused on a yacht off the port bow, and the sun’s glare on the starboard bow would have made Phoenix very difficult to see.
- Page 4: In addition to watching the yacht, the chief officer would also have been concentrating on steadying and keeping the ferry on its new heading.

report_title: MAIB Report 4/2019 - Red Falcon and Phoenix - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown, multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Sun glare lies along a contact's bearing despite otherwise good visibility.
- Sun blinds are left unused because a course alteration is expected shortly.
Investigator finding: Glare made Phoenix very difficult to see, and not lowering the bridge sun screens reduced lookout effectiveness.
Transferable lesson: Treat glare as a local impairment of visual detection and use available glare mitigation; an imminent alteration does not remove the need for effective lookout on the present heading.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The glare-specific lesson does not transfer where glare does not impair the relevant view.
- Use of bridge sun screens is not applicable where such equipment is absent.
Source quotations:
- Page 5: without the sun blinds, which were not used because of the imminent alteration of course to port, Phoenix would have been very difficult to see.
- Page 7: The effectiveness of the lookout maintained on Red Falcon’s bridge was reduced because the master and chief officer remained seated throughout the vessel’s transit through the Solent, and did not lower the bridge window sun screens.

report_title: MAIB Report 4/2019 - Red Falcon and Phoenix - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown, multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- The current operating position obscures close contacts behind window frames or the bow.
- Radar cannot be monitored effectively from the occupied control position.
- Visual lookout is impaired but is not supported by radar.
Investigator finding: Remaining seated increased visual obstructions and prevented effective radar monitoring; investigators identified standing and checking blind spots and radar as appropriate.
Transferable lesson: Check whether the current control position permits effective visual and radar monitoring; arrange lookout coverage to check blind spots and radar rather than relying on a fixed seated view.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The posture-specific analogy does not apply where the occupied position provides effective radar access and unobstructed relevant views.
- Radar checking is not available on vessels without radar.
Source quotations:
- Page 7: From their seated positions, the master and chief officer could not monitor radar targets or check the blind arcs created by the bridge’s window frames.
- Page 5: Given the bridge layout and the adverse impact of the sun on effective visual lookout, it would have been appropriate for at least one of the bridge team to stand up and frequently check blind spots and the radar.

report_title: MAIB Report 4/2019 - Red Falcon and Phoenix - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: overtaking
Vessel roles: stand_on
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- The helmsman looks only ahead while entering a channel.
- No other occupant is positioned to detect traffic approaching from astern.
Investigator finding: Phoenix's owner did not look astern when entering the channel at a shallow angle, and no passenger was positioned to see the approaching ferry.
Transferable lesson: Include astern sectors in the lookout when entering a traffic channel; looking ahead alone cannot establish whether an overtaking vessel is approaching.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The specific coverage failure is absent where an effective lookout already monitors astern and communicates approaching traffic.
Source quotations:

report_title: MAIB Report 4/2019 - Red Falcon and Phoenix - Serious Marine Casualty
text:

Vessel roles: stand_on

- There is no confirmation that the approaching vessel has detected own vessel or has room to manoeuvre.
Investigator finding: Although Phoenix's owner correctly understood the overtaking vessel's obligation to keep clear, his assumptions about detection and manoeuvring ability were misplaced.
Transferable lesson: Do not treat another vessel's keep-clear obligation as evidence that it has seen you or can manoeuvre clear; retain an active assessment of the developing encounter.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The overtaking-obligation analogy does not establish roles in crossing, head-on, or otherwise uncertain encounters.
- The finding does not support any particular avoiding manoeuvre.

report_title: MAIB Report 18/2018 - Celtic Spirit - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact, multi_contact
Vessel roles: not_applicable
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: delayed_action, other
Warning signs:
- Engine stopped or not immediately available to the bridge.
- Time to propulsion availability approaches time to nearby vessels.
- Limited alternative means of arresting anchor drag.
Investigator finding: Engine preparation consumed the remaining response time, and lack of a second anchor severely restricted the watchkeeper's options.
Transferable lesson: Assess actual propulsion availability and other available control measures against the time before drifting into nearby vessels; do not equate a plan to start the engine with immediate manoeuvring capability.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The engine-start delay mechanism does not apply where propulsion is already immediately available; other manoeuvring constraints still require separate assessment.
Source quotations:
- Page 8: As it took 17 minutes for control of the engine to be passed to the bridge, the 2/O would have needed to recognise that the vessel was dragging anchor almost immediately to have had a chance of preventing the first collision.
- Page 8: Without a second anchor to deploy, the 2/O’s options were extremely limited, and collision avoidance was almost solely reliant on other vessels getting out of Celtic Spirit’s way.
- Page 9: Celtic Spirit was unable to manoeuvre quickly because its engines were not on immediate readiness.

- Nearby vessels and VTS have not been alerted.
Investigator finding: The watchkeeper did not warn VTS or neighbouring vessels; an early warning might have given Celtic Warrior sufficient time to avoid the second collision, although the first might still have been unavoidable.
Transferable lesson: Promptly alert VTS and nearby vessels when dragging creates a collision threat so their preparation can begin without waiting for independent detection; do not assume a warning guarantees avoidance.

- The finding does not establish that an early broadcast always leaves enough time to escape, particularly for the nearest vessel.

report_title: MAIB Report 6/2018 - F4 Powerboats - Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD

Vessel roles: uncertain

Warning signs:
- High-speed operation in close proximity to another vessel.
- Sudden, unexpected loss of directional control by a nearby vessel.
Investigator finding: Boat 22 probably changed direction because of a structural hull failure; the vessels' speed and proximity then left no opportunity to avoid collision.
Transferable lesson: When assessing close-proximity, high-speed operation, account for the possibility that an unexpected loss of directional control could leave insufficient time to react; do not assume a nearby vessel will maintain its intended track.
Do not transfer this analogy when:

- It does not establish that a collision would be unavoidable where greater separation or different speeds allow time to respond.

Encounter types: unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Both radar displays set to the same long range.
- Small, close, almost stationary contact.
- Drifting contact has no radar trail.
Investigator finding: The common 6-mile scale made the drifting craft harder to detect; different scales would have supported both distant scanning and close-contact monitoring.
Transferable lesson: With two radar displays available, use complementary ranges for distant and nearby traffic, and give close attention to small contacts that may show no trail.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The two-display arrangement does not transfer directly to a single-display installation.
- The particular detection difficulty depends on contact size, motion, range and display scale; six miles is not inherently unsuitable in every situation.
Source quotations:
- Page 10: James 2 was drifting and therefore would not have been presenting a trail on Vertrouwen’s radar screens.
- Page 11: The 6-mile range set on Vertrouwen’s radar screens made it more difficult for the skipper to detect the drifting James 2.
- Page 10: A better practice, with two displays available, would have been to set them at different range scales so as to achieve both long range scanning and monitoring of any contacts close by.

report_title: MAIBInvReport 24/2017 - Typhoon Clipper and Alison - Very Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: multi_contact, unknown
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_team_coordination, other
Warning signs:
- A vessel is entering busy traffic without making its plan apparent.
- Nearby vessels may not have detected the departing craft.
Investigator finding: Alison’s crew did not indicate their intentions to nearby vessels; the analysis identified available radio and visual means of doing so.
Transferable lesson: Before committing to movement into busy traffic, make intentions apparent using appropriate available communication rather than relying on others to infer the plan.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- Communication does not itself establish that the proposed movement is safe or replace collision-risk assessment.
- The suggested visual communication depends on first gaining the other vessel’s attention.
Source quotations:
- Page 13: Alison’s crew made no attempt to indicate their intentions to other vessels nearby in a busy part of the waterway.
- Page 11: There was a hand-held VHF radio on board that could have been used to inform the other vessels of the workboat’s plan.
- Page 11: having gained the attention of Typhoon Clipper’s master, made a visual signal giving warning of the plan to pass ahead.

report_title: MAIBInvReport 24/2017 - Typhoon Clipper and Alison - Very Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: unknown, multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing, action_required
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- A small contact passes behind a pier or other obstruction.
- The contact can move directly from external obstruction into the vessel’s own blind sector.
Investigator finding: Alison was initially hidden by the pier and then entered Typhoon Clipper’s forward blind sector, preventing wheelhouse line-of-sight detection.
Transferable lesson: Account for both external obstructions and own-vessel blind sectors when assessing whether the intended movement area has actually been observed clear.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The report’s visibility distances are specific to these vessels and must not be applied to other vessel geometries.
- This is an obstruction and blind-sector lesson, not a finding about meteorological restricted visibility.
Source quotations:
- Page 11: once Alison had passed the end of the pier, it entered Typhoon Clipper’s visual blind sector ahead and all possibility of a line of sight detection from Typhoon Clipper’s wheelhouse was lost.
- Page 13: Neither the master nor mate of Typhoon Clipper saw Alison because it was initially obscured by the pier, then moved into the visual blind sector ahead and the CCTV settings excluded use of the bow camera.

report_title: MAIBInvReport 24/2017 - Typhoon Clipper and Alison - Very Serious Marine Casualty
text:

Investigator finding: The bow camera recorded Alison and covered the forward blind spot, but its image was excluded from the wheelhouse display configuration.

report_title: MAIB Report 14/2025 - Isabell Princess of the Sea/Vega - Very Serious Marine Casualty
text:
MAIB INVESTIGATION LESSON CARD
Encounter types: stationary_contact, multi_contact
Vessel roles: uncertain
Encounter phases: monitoring, risk_developing
Causal mechanisms: poor_monitoring
Warning signs:
- Recent departure from a lit environment at night
- Failure to detect an anchored vessel until signalled
Investigator finding: The helm's night vision was still developing, and the failure to detect the gulet also evidenced impaired night vision. Neither person responsible aboard the tender saw Vega in time.
Transferable lesson: Account for incomplete dark adaptation when assessing whether visual lookout can detect hazards in time; responding to one visible contact does not demonstrate that all nearby contacts have been detected.
Do not transfer this analogy when:
- The dark-adaptation mechanism does not transfer to daylight encounters or establish impaired vision in an already dark-adapted observer.
Source quotations:
- Page 9: whose eyes would still have been developing their night vision
